claims.text: The proposed framework combines machine-learning-enhanced DFT with Boltzmann transport theory.
The framework can decouple lattice and electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Its channel-specific predictions will be approximately 30% more accurate than predictions from Debye-temperature-based or bulk-averaged approaches.
The target material is bulk, single-phase crystalline HfNbTaTiZr with controlled oxygen content.
The method explicitly calculates separate mode-resolved scattering rates for phonons and electrons.
Machine-learning adjustments to DFT inputs can better capture local disorder and impurity effects.
The method is valid below 200 K for separately resolving lattice and electronic contributions.
The method is valid from 300 to 1200 K for predicting total conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Mass variation, force-constant variation, and localized oxygen scattering are relevant atomic-scale mediators of transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Phonon transport can be modeled using scattering rates that include anharmonicity and impurity scattering.
Electronic transport can be modeled using scattering rates that account for conduction-band properties and disorder-induced localization.
The predicted lattice and electronic conductivities will sum to total high-temperature conductivities of 10–17 W/(K m).
Earlier approaches used defect-free bulk crystals and simplified bulk-averaged or Debye-temperature-based parameters.
Earlier approaches conflated phonon and electronic heat-transport contributions.
Below 200 K, phonon and electronic heat-transport channels are independently measurable.
High impurity concentrations or extreme compositional inhomogeneity may cause significant model deviations.
Nonlinear impurity-scattering effects, phase transitions, and uncontrolled compositional fluctuations may limit prediction accuracy.
Minimal-oxygen and controlled 1 wt.% oxygen specimens provide comparison groups for testing impurity effects.
Deviation of either predicted channel or their sum by more than ±30% from experiment falsifies the hypothesis.
Failure to observe clear separation of lattice and electronic transport below 200 K falsifies the hypothesis.
